Q432.L1t: State laws governing who may appear on an election ballot are subject to limits imposed by the Fourteenth Amendment.
Q432.L2t: The Supreme Court has reviewed candidate filing requirements and ballot-access rules in cases such as Williams v. Rhodes and Lubin v. Panish.
Q432.L3t: A law that burdens the fundamental rights to vote and to run for office is reviewed under strict scrutiny, where the government rather than the challenger must show the law is necessary to a compelling interest.
Q432.L4t: The most probable outcome is that the court will require the state to justify the heavier signature requirement for new entrants, not make the resident prove it invalid.
Q432.L2f: Signature requirements for ballot access were first adopted by states only after the year 2000, so courts have little precedent on them.
Q432.L3f: The signature rule treats all new entrants alike, so it creates no classification or burden on voting rights, but it arbitrarily takes away a candidate's protected liberty interest in seeking office through an unfair procedure.
Q432.L4f: The most probable outcome is that the court will strike down the requirement because it denies the candidate due process of law under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Q437.L1t: Abdominal masses are assessed clinically by inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.
Q437.L2t: When a pulsatile abdominal mass is found, an examiner must decide whether the pulsation is expansile or merely transmitted from the aorta beneath.
Q437.L3t: Stool-filled bowel is soft and putty-like, so a finger pressed into it leaves a dent that persists, which does not happen with solid tumours or organs.
Q437.L4t: A mass that can be indented by finger pressure is explained by faeces loading the colon.
Q437.L2f: Abdominal aortic aneurysms almost always cause severe pain and are rarely found without symptoms.
Q437.L3f: Only an aneurysm can produce pulsation in an abdominal mass, because any other mass lying over the aorta is unable to transmit the aortic beat.
Q437.L4f: Any pulsatile abdominal mass can be concluded to be an aneurysm of the aorta.

Q436.L1t: The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure contain rules on joinder of parties and on intervention by non-parties.
Q436.L2t: Rule 24 recognizes two kinds of intervention, as of right and permissive, and each requires a timely motion.
Q436.L3t: Under Rule 24(b) a court may, in its discretion, let a timely applicant intervene when its claim and the main action have a question of law or fact in common, and both claims here arise from the same fall and the same alleged negligence.
Q436.L4t: The court is likely to allow the employer to intervene because its property claim arises from the same incident and turns on the same negligence issues as the clerk's claim.
Q436.L2f: Intervention in federal court is available only to persons who were named in the original complaint and must be sought before the defendant answers.
Q436.L3f: Because the employer's property damage came from the same accident, the court cannot give complete relief or proceed fairly without the employer, so the action cannot go forward in its absence.
Q436.L4f: The court is likely to grant the motion because the action cannot properly proceed without the employer being brought into it as a necessary party.
